This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis.
It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition.
A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.
Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money.
A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them.
What would Prop. 1 do?
If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes.
Where would the money go?
Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down:
$7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
$1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes.
$1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes.
$500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements.
$450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing.
$350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students.
$200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation.
$200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing.
How would California pay for it?
It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments.
Have we done anything like this before?
California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1.
What do supporters say?
Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires.
Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that.
Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis.
“Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.”
What do opponents say?
When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers.
Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets.
“It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing.
And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said.
Opponents have not reported receiving any contributions.

I need to research cost-effectiveness, California's budget, past bond performance, and whether this is the right tool.

The case for yes is strong. California faces a severe housing shortage with 2.2 million low-income households competing for 664,000 affordable rentals and over 180,000 homeless. Nearly 40,000 approved units are stalled without gap financing. The bond would unlock this pipeline. Prop 1 in 2018 produced roughly 22,735 units and was fully committed by 2023.

State general fund housing funding has dried up due to budget deficits. The bond is the traditional mechanism for capital investment.

The cost is modest at roughly 0.25% of the general fund or $500–600 million annually. The interest premium is only about 15% after inflation, making it relatively efficient borrowing.

The veterans portion is self-financing through CalVet and has historically required no taxpayer cost. It has helped nearly a million veterans.

Affordability covenants run for 55 years, ensuring units serve multiple generations.

The bond leverages federal LIHTC and other matching funds, so bond dollars are not the full cost. It has bipartisan legislative support with no formal opposition campaign. It does not raise taxes directly; instead it spreads the cost of long-lived capital assets over 25 to 55 years. The measure also covers preservation, supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker, tribal, and student housing.

California YIMBY supports the measure. They generally favor supply-side reforms over subsidy-only approaches.

The case against is also significant. California faces structural budget deficits. The $500–600 million annual debt service would crowd out education and health priorities. Taxpayers already pay roughly $6 billion annually on $80 billion in existing bond debt.

It does not fix root causes like CEQA, zoning, high construction costs, prevailing wage laws, or impact fees. Subsidized housing in California costs $500,000 to over $1 million per unit.

The Los Angeles Times, East Bay Times, San Luis Obispo Tribune, and Skelton have all opposed the measure. They argue that borrowing cannot solve the housing crisis and that the bond is a special interest potpourri.

Only 11 percent of the veterans portion actually goes to veterans. They repay their own loans through CalVet.

The bond also feeds the existing fragmented affordable housing finance system rather than streamlining it. The Los Angeles County Office of Education has recommended consolidating these programs.

The Terner Center notes this is not a bill to make housing affordable. Subsidies are second-best if regulatory reform could unlock more market housing. Bonds defer taxes and add interest costs that pay-as-you-go projects avoid. The money is split across farmworkers, tribes, students, and veterans to build a coalition rather than maximize units per dollar. Student housing would cost roughly $292,000 per bed.

Homeownership assistance could bid up prices if supply is constrained. Past bonds have not solved the crisis because the shortage is huge relative to bond size and regulatory barriers persist. I still need to check per-unit costs, budget deficit projections, debt capacity, the LAO streamlining report, and program effectiveness.

I am checking the bond text for accountability and prevailing wage issues that could inflate costs. The best policy judgment is yes, with caveats. Market reforms alone cannot serve extremely low-income households.

Public subsidy is the standard global tool for that gap. The marginal cost is small relative to the state budget and the assets last 55 years. Borrowing for long-lived capital is sound public finance when the state lacks surplus cash. The stalled pipeline of roughly 40,000 permitted units is concrete, not speculative. This offers unusually high certainty compared to many bonds.

The 2018 bond was fully deployed and produced tens of thousands of units. The programs are not untested.

The veterans CalVet portion is essentially free to taxpayers and has a long successful history. Even critics do not oppose that part, and you cannot vote for only that portion.

There is no organized opposition with a better alternative on the ballot. Prop 45 might be complementary rather than a substitute. Regulatory reform alone cannot house people earning $20,000 per year when even cheap apartments cost more than 30 percent of their income.

The argument that the bond will not solve the crisis is a nirvana fallacy. A meaningful increment of 40,000 units plus preservation and homeownership assistance still matters. Policy should be judged on whether benefits exceed costs, not whether it solves everything.

Cost-effectiveness concerns are real. California housing is expensive per unit due to labor rules, fees, financing complexity, and land costs. Rejecting the bond does not lower those underlying costs; it simply means those 40,000 units will not be built. The legislature has been passing streamlining laws separately.

The $500–600 million annual debt service is roughly 0.25 percent of the general fund, which is manageable against a budget over $200 billion. Existing debt service is about three percent of the budget. The structural deficit is a concern, but housing capital investment yields positive fiscal externalities by reducing expensive homelessness costs such as shelter, emergency room visits, and policing.

The Los Angeles County Office of Education estimates the bond would provide roughly $180,000 in gap financing per unit. That is a reasonable leverage ratio against full construction costs of $600,000 to $800,000. Farmworker and student housing are more expensive per unit but represent smaller shares.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Endorsement : Who should replace Nancy Pelosi in Congress? It’s not even a choice (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

10/02/26

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. # Proposition 37
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges.
The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects.
Over time, investors are repaid with interest.
The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds.
The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund.
(The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
...
### Proposal
***Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program.*** Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds.
CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.”
Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price.
(Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.)
Homeowners’ monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program’s administrative costs.
CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible.
CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.

The state repays $80 billion in bonds at a 3% rate, below the historical 4%. Prop 1 adds only 0.25% of general fund revenue. The $10 billion bond would cover the $2.3 billion pipeline gap and fund future production. I am also checking the California budget deficit outlook.

The $10 billion bond is reasonable relative to the documented gap. MHP has nine requests per dollar available, confirming real oversubscription. State funding leverages roughly $3.60 of private capital per dollar. The average state subsidy of about $170,000 per rental home is a sensible gap financing mechanism. California development costs are two to four times higher than in Texas or Colorado, but the bond still prevents units from remaining unbuilt.

The Chronicle, SPUR, California YIMBY and McClatchy editorial boards support the bond. The Mercury News, East Bay Times and Skelton oppose it. No formal anti-campaign exists. The Legislature is heavily in favor with 29 of 40 Senate and 61 of 80 Assembly votes.

The LAO projects multi-year structural deficits. Adding $550 million in annual debt service is small but real. The strongest no argument is that California's housing finance system is inefficient and per-unit costs are extremely high, so borrowing $10 billion would lock in a bad production model for 25 years.

The strongest yes argument is that low-income housing requires subsidy regardless of regulatory reform. The pipeline is shovel-ready and programs are proven. Recent reforms improve cost-effectiveness going forward.

I recommend voting yes. The problem is severe and documented. The fiscal cost is modest and debt load is below historical norms. The mechanism matches the problem.

The self-financing veterans component is clearly beneficial. Voting no leaves the pipeline stalled and produces no better alternative. Regulatory reform is complementary but not a substitute. I am weighing social benefits against costs for an overall judgment.

The bond would build up to 40,000 rental units and 40,000 homeownership assists. It would also fund 2,500 farmworker units, 1,200 student beds, and 2,100 veteran loans at no taxpayer cost. Supportive housing for homelessness would receive $1.15 billion. The annual cost is roughly $500 million to $600 million from the general fund over 25 years. That equals about $13 billion to $15 billion in nominal terms. The real premium is approximately 15 percent.

The opportunity cost of using general fund money for this bond is significant. It could otherwise fund education, health care, debt reduction, or tax relief. The bond will not lower market rents much. Some programs may carry inefficiency or pork. The fiscal cost works out to roughly $14,000 per rental unit annually for 25 years. That is a substantial ongoing public burden.

The $14,000 annual cost per rental unit is roughly in line with the existing rent gap between market and affordable housing. The $550 million in debt service covers the full $10 billion bond rather than just the $7.2 billion allocated to rental units. At the implied rate, that equals about $9,900 in annual debt service per rental unit over 25 years.

The annual $14,000 cost per rental unit is reasonable compared to the $30,000-plus yearly cost of chronic homelessness services. I have completed my research and am ready to answer.

The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. OVERVIEW OF STATE BOND DEBT
This section describes the state’s bond debt. It also discusses how the bond measures on the
ballot, if approved by voters, would affect state costs to repay bonds.
State Bonds and Their Costs
What Are Bonds? Bonds are a way that governments borrow money. The state government
uses bonds primarily to pay for infrastructure projects that have a long useful life, such as
bridges, dams, prisons, parks, schools, and office buildings. The state sells bonds to investors to
receive up-front funding for these projects and then must repay the investors over a period of
time, typically a couple of decades. This is very similar to the way a family pays off a mortgage
on their home.
What Are the Costs of Bond Financing? The state’s total cost for a project is more if it pays
with bonds than if it pays up front with money it already has. This is because it has to pay
interest on the bonds. The amount of additional cost depends on the interest rate and how long it
takes to repay the bonds. For example, if the state uses a 30-year bond with a 4 percent interest
rate to pay for a project, the total cost is about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than
if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Most Bonds Must Be Approved by Voters. The State Constitution requires that most new
bonds be approved by voters. These bonds usually are repaid from the state General Fund. (The
General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education,
health care, and prisons.)
Bonds and State Spending
Current Amount of Bond Debt. The state currently is repaying about $80 billion of bonds
from the state General Fund. In addition, the voters and the Legislature previously have approved
about $40 billion of General Fund-supported bonds that have not yet been sold. Most of these
bonds are expected to be sold in the next several years. The state currently is paying about
$6 billion each year from the General Fund to repay bonds. The state will continue to pay a
similar amount over the next few years. This is about 3 percent of the state’s annual General
Fund revenue, which is lower than the historical average of about 4 percent.
This Election’s Impact on Debt Payments. There are two General Fund-supported bond
measures on this ballot: Proposition 1 and Proposition 38. Proposition 1 would allow the state to
borrow $10 billion for affordable housing programs. The cost to repay this bond would be about
$500 million to $600 million each year for 25 years. Proposition 38 would allow the state to
borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. The cost to repay this bond
would be about $500 million to $600 million each year for 20 years. The cost to repay both

Proposition 1: California’s Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond
A $11.25 Billion Bond to Continue Building Affordable Homes for Californians
July 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 1, appearing on the November 2026 ballot, would provide funding for affordable housing and accessible homeownership. Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a $11.25 billion general obligation bond to fund programs that support the creation and preservation of affordable housing, expand homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income Californians and veterans, and invest in permanent solutions to solve homelessness. If Prop. 1 is approved, it would replenish funding for several successful state programs that have exhausted their resources. Prop. 1 was placed on the ballot by the Legislature through passage of Senate Bill 417 (2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417).
table of contents
How Has California Expanded Affordable Housing & What Gaps Remain?
Why Is Affordable Housing Funding Running Out & How Would Prop. 1 Help?

Prop. 1 Supporters and Opponents
How Has California Expanded Affordable Housing & What Gaps Remain?
Over the past six years, California has nearly tripled (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/CHP_2026-Housing-Needs-Report-FINAL.pdf) the number of new affordable homes it funds. Yet the state continues to face a severe shortage of affordable housing, particularly for Californians with the lowest incomes. California needs more than 2.5 million new homes, including at least 1 million homes that are affordable to lower-income households. Housing cost pressures fall hardest on California renters as nearly half pay unaffordable rents — a hardship that disproportionately impacts Black and Latinx renters with low incomes, older adults, mixed-status families, and people with disabilities.
Unlike market-rate or luxury housing, affordable housing projects typically cannot be built without subsidies because affordable rents do not generate enough revenue to cover development or operating costs. As a result, affordable housing projects rely on multiple funding streams to close financing gaps. Currently, more than 46,000 affordable homes across California (491 developments) (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2024-04/State_Pipeline_2024_FINAL.pdf) are waiting for the last bit of state funding needed to break ground. Prop. 1 would provide funding for various programs that help bridge the financial gap to keep affordable housing construction moving.
Why Is Affordable Housing Funding Running Out & How Would Prop. 1 Help?
Despite the ongoing housing affordability challenges Californians are facing, state funding for affordable housing has largely disappeared. Over the past several years, affordable housing programs have relied on one-time General Fund investments (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/protecting-progress-state-housing-and-homelessness-funding-must-continue/) to supplement voter-approved housing bonds, but those investments have drastically declined. The 2026 Budget Act only includes one-time investments in two significant affordable housing programs: $500 million for state Low Income Housing Tax Credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program, effectively leaving multiple programs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/first-look-understanding-the-governors-proposed-2026-27-california-budget/#h-proposed-budget-includes-no-new-state-funding-for-affordable-housing) without additional funds. Beyond these investments, there is no meaningful ongoing or one-time investment from the state General Fund for affordable housing development.
The state’s remaining modest affordable housing funding sources, including the Affordable Housing and Sustainable Communities Program (AHSC), funded through Cap-and-Invest; state and federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits; and SB 2 planning funds are insufficient to meet the demand and often require additional funding to be fully leveraged. The AHSC program was expected to receive nearly $800 million per year for affordable housing, but recent changes by the California Air Resources Board put that funding at risk.
Curious About Other Ballot Propositions?
Browse our collection of resources covering California’s statewide ballot measures to help you understand what’s at stake for California this November.
See More Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/)
The funding approved by voters through the 2018 Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act has been fully committed — exhausted within five years, by the end of 2023, due to overwhelming demand. The state’s flagship Multifamily Housing Program, which relied on funding from the bond and one-time General Fund investments, is routinely oversubscribed by roughly 9 to 1. Together these signal that the barrier to building more affordable housing in California isn’t a lack of will or projects — it’s a lack of sustainable funding.
Without new state investments, affordable housing production will stall just as California is making meaningful progress and as federal cuts threaten to make it even more difficult for Californians to make ends meet, which is why state lawmakers placed Prop. 1 on the ballot.
What Affordable Housing and Homeownership Programs Would Prop. 1 Fund?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize $11.25 billion in general obligation (GO) bonds that would support the construction and preservation of affordable rental homes, expand homeownership assistance for low- and moderate-income homebuyers, including veterans, and provide permanent housing for people at risk of or experiencing homelessness. Within these categories, it would provide some funding for programs that serve distinct populations, such as California tribes, farmworkers, unhoused youth, and college students. The bond funds would be allocated as follows:
Affordable Housing Development and Preservation
$5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program (MHP) , which supports the construction, rehabilitation, or preservation of affordable rental housing. At least 10% of units in a MHP development must be available for extremely low-income households who are at the highest risk of facing homelessness. This is one of California’s model affordable housing development programs.
$1.15 billion for supportive housing through the MHP program. Supportive housing provides stable homes with wrap-around services for people who were chronically homeless or at risk of becoming so. These funds can be used for operating subsidy reserves, which are critical to the longevity and sustainability of permanent supportive housing.
Up to 15% — $150 million — would be allocated as grants to acquire or build permanent supportive housing among other specified uses.
Another $150 million is carved out for the capital development or acquisition of youth housing through MHP. This would serve current or former foster youth, homeless minors or youth, or youth at risk of homelessness.
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program, which provides funding to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded rental multifamily housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program . This would provide incentive grants to assist with new construction and rehabilitation of infrastructure that supports high-density affordable and mixed-income housing in locations designated as infill.
$450 million for the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.
$350 million for affordable student housing projects to be split evenly between the University of California and the California State University.
$200 million for a new Community Anti-Displacement and Preservation Program, which helps protect unsubsidized housing that may naturally be affordable and requires long-term affordability regulations.
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program which finances housing and housing-related activities to enable tribes to rebuild and reconstitute their communities.
$200 million to the Affordable Housing Innovation Fund for the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program. This would fund competitive grants or loans to local housing trust funds that develop, own, lend, or invest in affordable housing and would be used to create pilot programs to demonstrate innovative approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.
Homeownership
$1.25 billion for the CalVet Home Loan Program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) to help veterans and their families purchase homes. This portion of the bond would be repaid through mortgage (principal and interest) payments.
$600 million for the CalHome program. CalHome provides forgivable loans for lower-income households in self-help homeownership projects, including subdivisions and manufactured homes.
$500 million for the My Home downpayment assistance program to fund low-to-moderate income home purchase assistance programs.
What Benefits Would Prop. 1 Create for California’s Economy & Communities?
Prop. 1 would help expand and preserve California’s affordable housing supply while generating economic benefits and advancing the state’s housing goals. The bond would help close the financing gap for affordable rental homes, which serve lower-income California families and include seniors, people with disabilities, farmworkers, college students, and unhoused youth. According to legislative analyses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), the bond is expected to:
Produce more than 40,000 new affordable homes for lower-income families and individuals.
Preserve more than 5,500 existing affordable homes , ensuring they remain affordable for future generations.
Create more than 53,000 construction jobs through building new housing across the state.
Generate $1.3 billion in state and local tax revenue that supports local communities and public services.
Every $1 invested in state affordable housing leverages roughly $4 (https://roadmaphome.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Roadmap-Home-Report-2026.pdf) in federal, local, and private investment, maximizing the impact of public dollars. Affordable housing also delivers economic, health, and environmental benefits (https://affordablehomes.calhousingpartnership.org/). For example:
Children who grow up in affordable housing earn a median of $51,000 more over their lifetimes,
Permanent supportive housing saves an estimated $1.80 in public costs for every $1 invested (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8863642/pdf/nihms-1768403.pdf), and
Building homes near jobs and transit lowers transportation costs while reducing greenhouse gas emissions (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/policy-and-research/intersectional-policy-work/housing-and-climate-change).
Together, these investments would expand housing opportunities, reduce housing instability, strengthen local economies, and help California meet its long-term housing needs.
How Would Prop. 1 Be Repaid?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a total of $11.25 billion in GO bonds, divided as follows:
A $10 billion GO bond for affordable housing and homeownership programs that would be repaid from the state’s General Fund, and
A $1.25 billion veterans’ bond, a type of tax-exempt GO bond, for the CalVet Home Loan program that would be repaid through mortgage payments, with the General Fund as a backstop.
California voters often pass GO bonds to fund infrastructure projects that are designed to serve the public over many generations, as has been the case with affordable housing. Voters have also historically passed veterans’ bonds for CalVet to support homeownership opportunities for veterans.
GO bonds are repaid from the state’s General Fund. Repaying the $10 billion bond would cost $580 million per year for the next 30 years, for a total estimated cost of $17.4 billion ($10 billion in principal and $7.39 billion in interest). As of the governor’s proposed 2026-27 budget, California had $6.3 billion in General Fund debt service for GO bonds, or roughly 2.6% of General Fund expenditures.
In contrast, veterans bonds are generally self-supporting because they are repaid through principal and interest payments made by CalVet Home Loan Program borrowers. However, they are still GO bonds and are ultimately backed by the state’s General Fund. If program revenues were insufficient to cover the debt service, the General Fund would be responsible for the difference. It is unclear how often, if ever, the General Fund has had to backfill debt payments for previous veterans bonds.
Prop. 1 bond dollars would replenish depleted affordable housing programs. But bond dollars alone will not solve the housing shortage, nor would they replace the need for ongoing investments to meet the state’s substantial housing needs.
Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 Draw From Same Bonding Capacity, Face Important Trade Offs
Voters face two GO bond measures on the November 2026 ballot: Prop. 1 and Proposition 38. Prop. 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in GO bonds to support research and development in immunology and immunotherapy. Voters should weigh how each proposal addresses the state’s most pressing needs, fits within California’s limited borrowing capacity, and affects the state’s ability to invest in services that help families today and in the future.
Like all GO bonds, Prop. 38 would require long-term General Fund debt-service payments — estimated at $500 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) for 25 years — reducing budget and bonding capacity for other state priorities. If both Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 are approved, it would reduce General Fund dollars by roughly $1.1 billion annually.
Public sector investment in scientific research is needed, particularly given federal cuts, but Prop. 38 raises important fiscal and policy considerations. GO bonds are conventionally used to finance infrastructure projects — like roads, bridges, or housing — that can be used over decades, roughly matching the time it takes to repay the bond itself.
Funding research through GO bonds does not work the same way. Bond-funded research gets most of the dollars upfront for grants, salaries, and operating costs, but are not guaranteed to be built into a lasting asset. Research findings do compound overtime, but the bond dollars themselves are depleted after a few years. The state then spends years or decades paying interest on bonds that stopped directly funding work long ago. So while scientific research needs funding, a GO bond is not the appropriate funding mechanism. Plus, half of Prop. 38’s funding would be concentrated on a limited set of health conditions, even though California already has multiple public and private research institutions (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) conducting work in these areas.
Prop. 1 doesn’t confront these same challenges. While previous affordable housing bond dollars were also used up quickly, they left behind affordable homes that will continue to serve numerous families for decades. Affordable housing developments that use state dollars must have affordability requirements for at least 55 years — way beyond the repayment of the bonds with which they’re financed. The community benefits and capital assets outlast the debt, which is the intended purpose of GO bonds.
Prop. 1 Supporters and Opponents
Prop. 1 is supported by a broad coalition (https://www.housingbondca.com/coalition) of organizations representing housing, business, labor, local government, older adults, tenants, homelessness, urban planning, construction, environmental, and civil rights interests, among others.
Official opposition has been limited. The primary opponents on record include a few Republican state legislators who voted against (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) placing the measure on the ballot.

by Max Dubler
Introduction
The 2026 Affordable Housing Bond – Proposition 1
This fall, California voters will vote on an $11.25 billion bond measure, Proposition 1, to fund housing programs, including Affordable Housing construction. California YIMBY recommends a “yes” vote on Prop 1.
This analysis is intended to explain what Affordable Housing is, how Prop 1 dollars will be used, and what effect the measure will have.
Analysis
What Does “Affordable Housing” Mean And How Is It Different From Housing Affordability?
When most people talk about “affordable housing” in casual conversation, they are referring to market rate housing that fits within their personal budget or homes that middle class people can afford. That is not how policymakers use this phrase.
In housing policy conversations, “Affordable Housing” is a technical term that refers to price-regulated housing for people making specified incomes (more on this in a moment). Affordable Housing properties usually have a covenant written into the property’s deed that requires the homes to be rented at certain levels of affordability, which is why you’ll sometimes hear Affordable Housing referred to as “deed-restricted Affordable Housing.” Most of this type of “affordable housing” is subsidized by the government, using revenues from taxes and bonds.
“Housing affordability,” on the other hand, refers to the relationship between your income and your rent. If your total monthly housing cost is below 30% of your income, your housing is considered “affordable” to you. If it’s between 30 and 50% of your monthly income, you are “cost burdened.” If it’s over 50% of your monthly income, you are “severely cost burdened.”
Researchers and policymakers measure housing affordability by comparing median incomes to median rents and home prices.
Subsidized Housing
Most housing subsidy programs work by paying the difference between 30% of a tenant’s income and the actual cost (amortized construction, finance, and operations/maintenance costs) of their housing. There are two main ways of doing this: vouchers, which subsidize rents for tenants in privately-owned housing; and Affordable Housing, where the building itself is subsidized.
The Housing Choice Voucher program, commonly known as Section 8 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_8_(housing)), is the largest federal housing subsidy program, serving about 2.3 million households (California YIMBY supports fully funding Section 8 (https://cayimby.org/resources/policy-framework/chapter-2/#fund-section-8).).
Section 8 vouchers subsidize voucher holders’ rent by paying landlords the difference between 30% of the tenant’s income, and the market-rate rent for their home. Only 10% of eligible families receive Section 8 vouchers (https://www.cbpp.org/research/housing/families-wait-years-for-housing-vouchers-due-to-inadequate-funding), both because the program is under-funded, and because the general shortage of market-rate housing makes it hard for voucher holders to find vacant homes. Los Angeles last opened the voucher wait list in 2022 (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/section-8-housing-choice-voucher-los-angeles-city-applications-lottery-hacla-affordable-homelessness), when it got 223,000 applications for 30,000 spots on the list (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/section-8-housing-choice-voucher-los-angeles-city-applications-lottery-hacla-affordable-homelessness).
Subsidized affordable housing, on the other hand, provides a subsidy to the physical housing structure itself. Tenants in Affordable Housing pay rent based on their incomes. Rent is usually set at 30% of the upper income limit for the unit.
There are different levels of affordability in Affordable Housing, which are set according to the tenant’s family size and income as it relates to the county-level area median income (AMI):
Moderate Income 80-120% of AMI
Low Income – 50-80% of AMI
Very Low Income – 30-50% of AMI
Extremely Low Income 0-30% of AMI
Different housing subsidies define incomes and rents slightly differently. You can see the income limits (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/ctcac/2026%20Income%20Limits%205-1-26%2B%20-%20ADA_0.pdf) and rent levels (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/ctcac/2026%20Rent%20Limits%205-1-26%2B%20-%20ADA_0.pdf) for various state and federal programs in California here (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/income-limits/state-federal-income-limits). Also, while there is some Affordable Housing for ownership, like Habitat for Humanity houses, most Affordable Housing is for rent.
Because rents are set at 30% of the upper limit of monthly incomes for the unit, many Affordable Housing tenants spend more than 30% of their incomes on rent, making them rent burdened.
The Vast Majority Of Low-Income Californians Do Not Live In Affordable Housing
84% of California’s lower-income households (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CHP_Unsubsidized-At-Risk-2026-FINAL_.pdf) live in unsubsidized, market-rate housing, not income-restricted Affordable Housing. There are about 600,000 total subsidized Affordable Housing units (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CHP_Subsidized-At-Risk-2026-FINAL.pdf) in California, making up about 4% of the state’s 14,880,000 total homes (https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT1Y2024.B25002?g=040XX00US06).
California YIMBY believes that we should help these low-income renters by increasing the supply of housing across the board to chip away at the housing shortage, which is the primary cause of unaffordable rents.
The Finance Gap, Or Why Affordable Housing Requires Funding
Before a new apartment is built, its investors and financers use a projection of rents and operating incomes to ensure the project will not lose money over the expected life of the building. Most of the time, the construction and development costs are paid off by a building’s rental income over the first 20 to 30 years of its life, after which rents cover ongoing maintenance and necessary upgrades.
However, lower-income tenants often cannot afford rents that are high enough to pay off the cost of building new homes. This creates a “financing gap” for people who want brand new apartments to be affordable to low-income tenants: someone has to pay the difference between the rents that these tenants can afford and the actual cost of building and maintaining homes for them.
There are two main ways of closing this gap: publicly-funded housing subsidies, and unfunded affordability mandates in new housing projects, which are often referred to as “inclusionary zoning” (IZ) requirements.
Unfunded Affordability Mandates Are Bad Policy (https://cayimby.org/resources/policy-framework/chapter-1/#subsidized-affordability) That Worsen The Housing Shortage
The stated intentions behind most inclusionary zoning (IZ) — the practice of requiring developers to offer a percentage of new housing units at below-market rents — are good. But cities routinely set the affordability requirements so high that building becomes financially infeasible (https://www.spur.org/news/2026-06-25/realigning-housing-policy-real-world-economics-san-francisco).
IZ mandates, unless accompanied by external subsidies, rely entirely on market rents to cross-subsidize affordable units, which homebuilders rent at a loss. This cross-subsidy only works if the market rents are high enough to produce the necessary surplus. In other words, IZ mandates are only workable when market rents far exceed the cost of construction, which only happens under conditions of housing scarcity.
In cases where market rents aren’t high enough to allow for cross-subsidization, landowners will usually opt out of building multifamily housing. Perversely, this meansIZ can actually exacerbate an area’s housing shortage (https://cayimby.org/blog/getting-by-on-reduced-supply-the-impact-of-affordability-mandates/) and lead to more displacement.
In fact, the very logic of IZ is flawed. The construction of more housing, including more market-rate housing, benefits the public by creating vacancies (https://cayimby.org/blog/movin-on-up-how-costly-new-homes-create-affordable-old-homes/) in the cheapest homes (https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/03/18/austins-surge-of-new-housing-construction-drove-down-rents). But IZ is premised on the notion that developers reap all the benefits from building new housing, and that the public needs a mechanism for extracting some benefit of its own. In the process, IZ ends up needlessly discouraging (https://cayimby.org/blog/the-tradeoffs-of-inclusionary-zoning-a-closer-look/) the production of a good that California needs more of. Further, IZ places the entire financial burden of funding subsidized housing on renters who live in multifamily housing while letting the truly wealthy — who overwhelmingly live in single-family homes they own — off the hook. (One analysis (https://cayimby.org/blog/california-cities-wanted-free-affordable-housing-turns-out-theres-a-huge-cost/) found that each inclusionary unit costs renters $800,000 in excess rent.)
Instead of requiring market rate renters to bear the cost of housing subsidies, the state should subsidize affordable housing itself.
This brings us to the Affordable Housing bond, which would provide significant funding for subsidized housing.
What Will This Bond Do?
If voters approve the bond, the state of California will issue $11.25 billion in general obligation debt, to be repaid from existing state tax receipts, and use the revenues to fund the following:
New Construction ($8.05 billion)
$5.1 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp), the main state fund for building Affordable apartment complexes.
$1.15 billion to supportive housing administered through the MHP program. “Supportive housing” is Affordable Housing with on-site social services, usually reserved for people leaving homelessness.
$600 million to the CalHOME Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/calhome), which supports for-sale Affordable Housing, often built by Habitat for Humanity.
$450 million to the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/fwhg).
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/tribes/thgp) for tribal housing.
$350 million for student housing, divided between the UC and CSU systems.
$200 million for an Affordable Housing Innovation Fund to support local pilot programs.
Acquiring, Upgrading, and Recapitalizing Existing Housing ($950 million)
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/prp), which renovates and re-capitalizes existing Affordable Housing.
$200 million for a program to be created by the Legislature that will buy existing market rate housing and convert it to Affordable Housing.
Other Purposes ($2.25 billion)
$500 million for the Home Purchase Assistance Fund to provide down payment assistance.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/iig), which funds things like sewer upgrades, street improvements, and site preparation necessary to facilitate affordable and mixed-income infill housing.
$1.25 billion for home loans for veterans.
So what will all this money do in practice?
The Infill Infrastructure Grant Program Is Good
Established in 2019, the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program provides state gap funding for capital improvement projects like sewer upgrades, street improvements, and site preparation necessary to facilitate affordable and mixed-income infill housing. Its purpose is to facilitate infill housing construction, and funding it is a good use of public money.
This brings us to the new construction funding, which is the bulk of the bond.
This Bond Will Build About 43,700 Affordable Homes
How many homes will this bond build? Affordable Housing developers expect to take the $8 billion in bond funding and leverage it to get about four times as much money from the federal government using the Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), a major source of Affordable Housing funding. A UC Berkeley analysis of Affordable Housing construction costs in California (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Low-Income-Housing-Tax-Credit-Construction-Costs-An-Analysis-of-Prevailing-Wages-August-2024.pdf) found that “in 2023, it cost approximately $708,000 to develop one [new construction] subsidized housing unit funded with Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) equity in California.” If we are able to secure federal funds and build at 2023’s development cost, the production funding in bond will produce about 57,000 new Affordable Homes for low-income Californians.
Given the increase in construction and interest costs since 2023, the Legislative Analyst’s Office estimate (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) that “the bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students” seems accurate.
$500 Million In Down Payment Assistance Could Drive Up Home Prices
California housing is expensive because there are not enough homes to accommodate everyone who wants to live here. Allocating $500 million for down payment assistance to help homebuyers buy existing homes on the open market will increase demand.
Absent new supply, this could increase competition for scarce housing and drive up home prices. The buyers who get the assistance will win, at the cost of driving up prices overall.
Investing $950 Million In Existing Housing Is Good, But Won’t Reduce Rents
Building lots of new homes is the only way to durably reduce housing costs across the board in high-demand regions like California.
Spending $950 million to rehabilitate existing Affordable Housing, and buy existing market rate housing and restrict the rents, will help the current and future residents of those buildings. But these funds will not expand the housing supply, and so will not bring down rents.
Pro-Housing Voters Should Vote Yes
Publicly-funded housing subsidies for low-income Californians who cannot afford market-rate rents are a good thing, and they should be more widely available (https://cayimby.org/resources/policy-framework/chapter-2#fund-section-8). Many of the programs this grant will fund are excellent. Pro-housing voters should vote YES on Prop 1.
To make sure we get as much value from this investment as possible, the state legislature should reduce the complexity of securing funding (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/blog/reducing-the-complexity-in-californias-affordable-housing-finance-system/) by offering true “one stop shop” financing for qualifying projects, create streamlined entitlement and permitting processes that do not impose additional costs, and use some of the Affordable Housing Innovation Fund money to fund the Affordable Housing portion of large projects subject to Inclusionary Zoning.
Policymakers should also follow the overwhelming evidence (https://www.buildingabundance.ca/p/vacancy-chains) that new market rate housing induces a “moving on up” effect that particularly benefits tenants in inexpensive older buildings (https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/03/18/austins-surge-of-new-housing-construction-drove-down-rents), and enact broad zoning and permitting reforms that will allow limited subsidy dollars to go further and help more tenants (https://cayimby.org/blog/how-a-boom-in-market-rate-housing-would-help-section-8-tenants/).
Further, the Affordable Housing industry should stop lobbying against (https://www.insidephilanthropy.com/home/philanthropy-needs-to-pick-a-side-on-the-housing-construction-debate) common-sense zoning and permitting reforms (https://cal.streetsblog.org/2021/05/19/parking-requirements-are-not-a-useful-bargaining-chip-for-increasing-affordable-housing) that will reduce housing costs by expanding the supply of new unsubsidized homes for middle-class families at no cost to taxpayers.

Research is complete. I am ready to decide.

The vote should be yes. The housing crisis is structural and severe. Over 2.2 million low-income households compete for 664,000 affordable rentals. More than 180,000 people are homeless. Eighty-four percent of low-income households live in unsubsidized housing.

Subsidy and zoning reform are complementary tools. California YIMBY supports the vote. The measure would unblock roughly 40,000 stalled units awaiting about $2.3 billion in state gap funding. The 2018 bond already delivered about 23,000 units. MHP is oversubscribed nine to one. This refills existing programs with a track record rather than creating new bureaucracy.

Each state dollar leverages roughly $3.60 to $4 in other funds. The 55-year affordability covenants mean the asset outlasts the debt, making this a sound use of general obligation bonds. The fiscal cost is manageable: about $500 million to $600 million per year for roughly 25 years, or 0.25 percent of general fund revenue. Current debt service is only 3 percent of revenue, below the historical average.

The state currently provides no general fund appropriations for housing production. The alternative to the bond is simply not building, not paying cash. CalVet at $1.25 billion is self-supporting and has a clean repayment history.

RAND correctly notes that California subsidized housing costs roughly 1.5 times market rate and four times Texas due to fees, timelines, and prevailing wage. The bond does not fix these underlying inefficiencies. However, rejecting it would leave shovel-ready projects unbuilt rather than lowering those costs.

Recent CEQA infill exemptions and financing-streamlining efforts improve the return on new dollars relative to past bonds. Supportive housing yields roughly $1.80 in public savings per dollar invested. Preserving existing affordable stock at $750 million is cheaper than new construction and prevents loss of that housing.

The no argument has no viable alternative. Borrowing will not solve the full shortage, but it still delivers tens of thousands of homes and hundreds of thousands of stable household-years. Cutting the budget is impossible because the legislature already zeroed out most housing general fund funding due to deficits. Capital housing has always required bonds because annual budgets cannot sustain it.
